--- title: "Univariate models" subtitle: "Stationarity, ARMA, SARIMA, ETS, Holt-Winters and a seasonal naive benchmark" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/setup.R") suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(tseries) # adf.test, jarque.bera.test library(urca) # ur.kpss library(uroot) # hegy.test library(lmtest) # coeftest library(FinTS) # ArchTest }) # Format a p-value for the text, including the relation sign ("= 0.0100", "< 2.2e-16") fmt_p <- function(p) { if (p < 2.2e-16) return("< 2.2e-16") if (p < 0.001) return(paste("=", format(p, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE))) paste("=", sprintf("%.4f", p)) } # KPSS statistics with the 5% critical value kpss_table <- function(x) { do.call(rbind, lapply(c("tau", "mu"), function(type) { t <- ur.kpss(x, type = type) data.frame( Specification = if (type == "tau") "Trend (tau)" else "Constant (mu)", Statistic = round(t@teststat, 4), `Critical value 5%` = t@cval[, "5pct"], check.names = FALSE ) })) } # ADF p-values for several lag orders (tseries reports p-values within [0.01, 0.99]) adf_lags <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 24) adf_table <- function(x) { data.frame( Lag = adf_lags, `p-value` = sapply(adf_lags, function(k) suppressWarnings(adf.test(x, k = k)$p.value)), check.names = FALSE ) } # HEGY statistics and p-values by frequency. The test regression includes a # constant, a linear trend and monthly dummies (deterministic = c(1, 1, 1)), and # the number of augmentation lags is chosen by BIC so that its residuals are not # autocorrelated. hegy_table <- function(x) { h <- hegy.test(x, deterministic = c(1, 1, 1), lag.method = "BIC", maxlag = 12) data.frame( Statistic = names(h$statistics), Value = round(h$statistics, 3), `p-value` = round(h$pvalues, 4), check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL ) } ``` ::: The series is the US Industrial Production Total Index (IPB50001N, 2017 = 100, not seasonally adjusted), monthly from January 1990 to April 2025 (424 observations). ## Visual analysis ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} autoplot(ip_ts) + labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![US industrial production, total index](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-ip-level-1.png){#fig-ip-level width=768} ::: ::: The series has a strong upward trend between 1990 and 2008, so its mean is not constant, which is a first sign of non-stationarity. Two major shocks stand out: the collapse during the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the very sharp but short-lived drop during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The trend and the level shifts call for formal unit root testing. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggtsdisplay(ip_ts) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Series, ACF and PACF in levels](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-ip-acf-1.png){#fig-ip-acf width=768} ::: ::: The ACF decays very slowly and almost linearly, staying far above the significance bands: the classic pattern of a non-stationary (unit root) process. The PACF has a large spike at lag 1 and significant spikes at the seasonal lags 12 and 24. Visually, the series needs both a regular difference (for the trend) and a seasonal difference at lag 12. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsubseriesplot(ip_ts) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Index (2017 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Seasonal subseries: one panel per month, blue line = monthly mean](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-subseries-1.png){#fig-subseries width=768} ::: ::: The monthly means differ: June and August have the highest average production, while April and July are lower. Unequal monthly means are visual evidence of a seasonal component, which motivates the HEGY test for seasonal unit roots. ## Stationarity tests in levels **KPSS** (null hypothesis: the series is stationary): ::: {#tbl-kpss-level .cell tbl-cap='KPSS test, series in levels'} ```{.r .cell-code} kpss_level <- kpss_table(ip_ts) kpss_level ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Specification | Statistic| Critical value 5%| |:-------------|---------:|-----------------:| |Trend (tau) | 1.2744| 0.146| |Constant (mu) | 5.3919| 0.463|
::: ::: In both specifications the statistic is far above the 5% critical value, so stationarity is rejected: the original series is non-stationary. **ADF** (null hypothesis: unit root) for several lag orders, and **Phillips-Perron**: ::: {#tbl-adf-level .cell tbl-cap='ADF p-values by lag order, series in levels'} ```{.r .cell-code} adf_level <- adf_table(ip_ts) pp_level <- PP.test(ip_ts) adf_level ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| p-value| |---:|---------:| | 1| 0.5683393| | 2| 0.6622783| | 3| 0.6272126| | 4| 0.7368886| | 5| 0.8011204| | 12| 0.3178361| | 24| 0.5213919|
::: ::: All ADF p-values are well above 0.05, so the unit root cannot be rejected. The Phillips-Perron test gives p = 0.5592 and leads to the same conclusion. KPSS, ADF and PP all agree that the series is non-stationary in levels. ## Seasonality test (HEGY) ::: {#tbl-hegy-level .cell tbl-cap='HEGY test on the log series (constant, trend and monthly dummies; lags chosen by BIC)'} ```{.r .cell-code} hegy_level <- hegy_table(log(ip_ts)) hegy_level ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Statistic | Value| p-value| |:---------|------:|-------:| |t_1 | -2.223| 0.4269| |t_2 | -4.368| 0.0002| |F_3:4 | 26.963| 0.0000| |F_5:6 | 15.272| 0.0000| |F_7:8 | 23.966| 0.0000| |F_9:10 | 23.543| 0.0000| |F_11:12 | 20.761| 0.0000| |F_2:12 | 23.620| 0.0000| |F_1:12 | 22.526| 0.0000|
::: ::: The HEGY test checks for unit roots at the zero frequency (`t_1`, an ordinary stochastic trend) and at each seasonal frequency (`t_2` and the F-statistics). Because the series has a trend and a seasonal pattern, the test regression includes a constant, a trend and monthly dummies. - For `t_1`, p = 0.4269 (> 0.05): the zero-frequency unit root is not rejected, so the series needs a regular (first) difference. - At all seasonal frequencies the p-values are below 0.01: seasonal unit roots are rejected. The seasonal pattern is **deterministic** (a stable pattern by month), not stochastic. Strictly, this points to a first difference with monthly dummies rather than a seasonal difference. The analysis below follows the usual SARIMA route with both a log transformation and a seasonal difference at lag 12, which is also what `auto.arima()` selects. Seasonally differencing a series without seasonal unit roots can over-difference it; this would show up as a seasonal MA coefficient close to −1 in the SARIMA model, which is checked below. ## Transformations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ip_log <- log(ip_ts) ip_seasonal_diff <- diff(ip_log, lag = 12) ip_stationary <- diff(ip_seasonal_diff) ``` ::: After the log transformation, the seasonal difference and a first difference, the unit root tests are repeated on the final series: ::: {#tbl-tests-stationary .cell tbl-cap='KPSS and ADF tests, stationary series'} ```{.r .cell-code} kpss_table(ip_stationary) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Specification | Statistic| Critical value 5%| |:-------------|---------:|-----------------:| |Trend (tau) | 0.0189| 0.146| |Constant (mu) | 0.0204| 0.463|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} adf_stationary <- adf_table(ip_stationary) pp_stationary <- PP.test(ip_stationary) adf_stationary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| p-value| |---:|-------:| | 1| 0.01| | 2| 0.01| | 3| 0.01| | 4| 0.01| | 5| 0.01| | 12| 0.01| | 24| 0.01|
::: ::: The KPSS statistics are now far below their 5% critical values, so stationarity is not rejected. All ADF p-values are 0.01, the smallest value `adf.test()` reports (the true p-value is lower), and Phillips-Perron gives p = 0.0100. The unit root is strongly rejected: the transformed series is stationary. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} autoplot(ip_stationary) + labs(x = "Year", y = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Stationary series: log, seasonal difference and first difference](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-stationary-1.png){#fig-stationary width=768} ::: ::: The transformed series no longer trends and fluctuates around zero. Higher volatility in 2008 and 2020 reflects the crisis episodes, but mean reversion is now clear. ## Train / test split ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_total <- length(ip_ts) n_train <- floor(0.75 * n_total) ip_train <- window(ip_ts, end = time(ip_ts)[n_train]) ip_test <- window(ip_ts, start = time(ip_ts)[n_train + 1]) ip_train_log <- window(ip_log, end = time(ip_log)[n_train]) h <- length(ip_test) ``` ::: The first 75% of the sample (318 months, to Jun 2016) is used to estimate the models; the last 106 months (Jul 2016 to Apr 2025) are kept for out-of-sample evaluation. The forecast horizon `h` equals the length of the test set, so RMSE, MAE and MAPE can be computed on it. ## ARMA models on the stationary series ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Same end date as the training set (June 2016), so no test months are used ip_stationary_train <- window(ip_stationary, end = time(ip_train)[n_train]) ggtsdisplay(ip_stationary_train) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Training part of the stationary series, ACF and PACF](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-arma-acf-1.png){#fig-arma-acf width=768} ::: ::: Short lags (1–4) are significant in both the ACF and PACF, which points to short-run AR and MA components. There are also large negative spikes at the seasonal lags 12 and 24, so a non-seasonal ARMA model will struggle to remove the autocorrelation at long lags. This is why several models are estimated and why SARIMA follows. ::: {#tbl-arma .cell tbl-cap='Candidate ARMA models on the stationary training series'} ```{.r .cell-code} arma_orders <- list(c(1, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 2), c(2, 0, 1)) arma_models <- lapply(arma_orders, function(o) Arima(ip_stationary_train, order = o)) arma_auto <- auto.arima(ip_stationary_train, seasonal = FALSE) arma_compare <- data.frame( Model = c(sapply(arma_orders, function(o) sprintf("ARMA(%d,%d)", o[1], o[3])), "auto.arima"), Specification = c(sapply(arma_models, function(m) as.character(m)), as.character(arma_auto)), AIC = round(c(sapply(arma_models, AIC), AIC(arma_auto)), 2), BIC = round(c(sapply(arma_models, BIC), BIC(arma_auto)), 2) ) arma_compare ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Model |Specification | AIC| BIC| |:----------|:-------------------------------|--------:|--------:| |ARMA(1,0) |ARIMA(1,0,0) with non-zero mean | -1952.14| -1940.97| |ARMA(0,1) |ARIMA(0,0,1) with non-zero mean | -1949.91| -1938.75| |ARMA(1,1) |ARIMA(1,0,1) with non-zero mean | -1971.19| -1956.31| |ARMA(1,2) |ARIMA(1,0,2) with non-zero mean | -1982.71| -1964.11| |ARMA(2,1) |ARIMA(2,0,1) with non-zero mean | -1978.86| -1960.26| |auto.arima |ARIMA(2,0,3) with zero mean | -1992.59| -1970.27|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} coeftest(arma_auto) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` z test of coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) ar1 -0.13977 0.10183 -1.3725 0.169898 ar2 0.61767 0.10267 6.0160 1.788e-09 *** ma1 0.21995 0.10586 2.0778 0.037728 * ma2 -0.42770 0.12627 -3.3873 0.000706 *** ma3 0.28867 0.06443 4.4804 7.451e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: `auto.arima()` selects ARIMA(2,0,3) with zero mean with AIC = -1992.59 and BIC = -1970.27, the lowest values among the candidates. The coefficients ar2, ma2 and ma3 are significant at 1% and ma1 at 5%; ar1 is not significant on its own but is kept to preserve the AR(2) structure. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arma_lb <- checkresiduals(arma_auto) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ljung-Box test data: Residuals from ARIMA(2,0,3) with zero mean Q* = 61.634, df = 19, p-value = 2.128e-06 Model df: 5. Total lags used: 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual diagnostics, ARMA model](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-arma-resid-1.png){#fig-arma-resid width=768} ::: ::: The Ljung-Box test gives p = 2.13e-06 (< 0.05), so the null hypothesis of independent residuals is rejected: the residuals are not white noise. The ACF confirms remaining autocorrelation at the seasonal lags 12 and 24. A non-seasonal ARMA model cannot capture the full dynamics of the series, which justifies moving to SARIMA. ## SARIMA ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_final <- auto.arima( ip_train_log, seasonal = TRUE, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE ) sarima_final ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Series: ip_train_log ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] Coefficients: ar1 ar2 ar3 sma1 0.0335 0.1736 0.2787 -0.6240 s.e. 0.0550 0.0545 0.0555 0.0459 sigma^2 = 6.284e-05: log likelihood = 1043.37 AIC=-2076.74 AICc=-2076.54 BIC=-2058.14 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coeftest(sarima_final) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` z test of coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) ar1 0.033529 0.055041 0.6092 0.542411 ar2 0.173565 0.054485 3.1855 0.001445 ** ar3 0.278703 0.055527 5.0192 5.189e-07 *** sma1 -0.624025 0.045860 -13.6072 < 2.2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: `auto.arima()` selects ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] on the log of the training data, with both a regular (d = 1) and a seasonal (D = 1) difference, as suggested by the analysis above. The fit improves considerably: AIC falls to -2076.74 (from -1992.59 for ARMA; both models are fitted to the same differenced training observations, so their AIC values are comparable). ar2, ar3 and the seasonal MA term sma1 are highly significant (p < 0.01); ar1 is kept for the consistency of the AR(3) structure. The seasonal MA coefficient, -0.62, is well away from −1, so there is no sign that the seasonal difference over-differences the series. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_lb <- checkresiduals(sarima_final) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ljung-Box test data: Residuals from ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] Q* = 16.173, df = 20, p-value = 0.7059 Model df: 4. Total lags used: 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual diagnostics, SARIMA model](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-sarima-resid-1.png){#fig-sarima-resid width=768} ::: ::: The Ljung-Box test gives p = 0.7059 (> 0.05): the residuals show no autocorrelation and behave like white noise. The seasonal MA term removed the correlation at lags 12 and 24, and the histogram is roughly symmetric. ### Further residual tests ::: {#tbl-sarima-tests .cell tbl-cap='Ljung-Box and ARCH tests on the SARIMA residuals'} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_resid <- residuals(sarima_final) lb_lags <- c(1:5, 8, 12, 24) sarima_lb_table <- data.frame( Lag = lb_lags, `Ljung-Box p-value` = sapply(lb_lags, function(l) { Box.test(sarima_resid, lag = l, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value }), check.names = FALSE ) arch_lags <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12) sarima_arch_table <- data.frame( Lag = arch_lags, `ARCH p-value` = sapply(arch_lags, function(l) ArchTest(sarima_resid, lags = l)$p.value), check.names = FALSE ) sarima_jb <- jarque.bera.test(sarima_resid) sarima_lb_table ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| Ljung-Box p-value| |---:|-----------------:| | 1| 0.9199917| | 2| 0.9918702| | 3| 0.9350804| | 4| 0.9727387| | 5| 0.9774096| | 8| 0.9858611| | 12| 0.9532487| | 24| 0.8817441|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_arch_table ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| ARCH p-value| |---:|------------:| | 1| 0.0001993| | 2| 0.0009375| | 4| 0.0004027| | 8| 0.0015016| | 12| 0.0000771|
::: ::: 1. **Autocorrelation (Ljung-Box):** all p-values are high (minimum 0.882), so the residuals are independent and the dynamics have been captured. 2. **Normality (Jarque-Bera):** p < 2.2e-16 (< 0.05), so normality is rejected. This is explained by turning points and major shocks (the 2008 crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 shock). 3. **Heteroscedasticity (ARCH):** p-values below 0.05 show ARCH effects (volatility clustering): the error variance is not constant, with larger residuals during episodes of macroeconomic instability. The model is valid for the conditional mean and is used for forecasting. ### SARIMA forecast ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Back-transform to index levels. The same model (same coefficients) is applied # to the series with lambda = 0, i.e. a log transformation, so forecast() # returns exp() of the log forecasts: the point forecast is the median of the # forecast distribution and the interval bounds (quantiles) carry over exactly. sarima_lvl <- Arima(ip_train, model = sarima_final, lambda = 0) sarima_real <- forecast(sarima_lvl, h = h) # For comparison: the bias-adjusted mean forecast sarima_mean <- forecast(Arima(ip_train, model = sarima_final, lambda = 0, biasadj = TRUE), h = h) sarima_mean_rmse <- accuracy(sarima_mean$mean, ip_test)[1, "RMSE"] autoplot(sarima_real) + autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") + labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![SARIMA forecast (back-transformed to index levels) against the test data](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-sarima-forecast-1.png){#fig-sarima-forecast width=768} ::: ::: 1. The forecasts are made for the log of the index and converted back with exp(). This gives the **median** forecast, and the prediction intervals stay valid because quantiles are preserved by exp(). The **mean** forecast would be higher by roughly half the forecast variance, which grows quickly with the horizon: the gap is 0.1 index points after 12 months but 8.3 after 106 months, and the RMSE on the test period would be 4.63 instead of 2.93. The median is used as the point forecast. 2. The forecast (blue) follows the centre of the test data (2016–2025) closely from this single origin; the rolling-origin evaluation below gives a more complete picture of out-of-sample performance. 3. The 2020 COVID-19 shock appears as a large exogenous deviation; the data later return to the forecast path. 4. The uncertainty fan widens asymmetrically, as expected for long-horizon forecasts on a log scale. ## Exponential smoothing (ETS) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ets_auto <- ets(ip_train, model = "ZZZ") ets_auto ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ETS(M,Ad,M) Call: ets(y = ip_train, model = "ZZZ") Smoothing parameters: alpha = 0.829 beta = 0.1046 gamma = 0.171 phi = 0.9789 Initial states: l = 61.6079 b = 0.0514 s = 0.9875 1 1.0138 1.0152 1.0081 0.9744 1.0172 0.9931 0.9909 1.0064 1.0037 0.9898 sigma: 0.0087 AIC AICc BIC 1666.886 1669.174 1734.603 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ets_lb <- checkresiduals(ets_auto) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ljung-Box test data: Residuals from ETS(M,Ad,M) Q* = 87.962, df = 24, p-value = 3.126e-09 Model df: 0. Total lags used: 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual diagnostics, ETS model](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-ets-resid-1.png){#fig-ets-resid width=768} ::: ::: The automatic selection gives ETS(M,Ad,M): multiplicative errors, an additive damped trend (φ = 0.9789) and multiplicative seasonality. The Ljung-Box test gives p = 3.13e-09 (< 0.05), so the residuals are not white noise, and the ACF shows remaining autocorrelation at short and seasonal lags (12, 24). In-sample, ETS leaves information in the residuals and is inferior to SARIMA in this respect, although out of sample the two models perform similarly (see the rolling-origin evaluation). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ets_forecast <- forecast(ets_auto, h = h) autoplot(ets_forecast) + autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") + labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ETS forecast against the test data](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-ets-forecast-1.png){#fig-ets-forecast width=768} ::: ::: 1. ETS reproduces the seasonal pattern but slightly underestimates the level over the test period. 2. The damped trend stabilises the central path and prevents unrealistic long-run growth. 3. The prediction intervals widen more slowly than for SARIMA: at the end of the test period (Apr 2025) the upper 95% bound is 158.4, compared with 220.5 for SARIMA. ## Holt-Winters ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hw_add <- hw(ip_train, seasonal = "additive", h = h) hw_mult <- hw(ip_train, seasonal = "multiplicative", h = h) hw_lo95 <- hw_add$lower[, "95%"] hw_first_negative <- time(hw_lo95)[which(hw_lo95 < 0)[1]] data.frame( Model = c("Additive", "Multiplicative"), AIC = round(c(hw_add$model$aic, hw_mult$model$aic), 2), `RMSE (train)` = round(c(accuracy(hw_add)[, "RMSE"], accuracy(hw_mult)[, "RMSE"]), 4), alpha = round(c(hw_add$model$par["alpha"], hw_mult$model$par["alpha"]), 4), check.names = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Model | AIC| RMSE (train)| alpha| |:--------------|-------:|------------:|------:| |Additive | 1705.07| 0.7760| 0.9216| |Multiplicative | 1847.54| 0.9614| 0.4711|
::: ::: 1. The additive model fits better in-sample than the multiplicative one, with a lower AIC and a lower training RMSE. 2. α = 0.9216 in the additive model means the level reacts strongly to the most recent shocks. 3. Limitation: in the forecast of the additive model over the test period, the lower 95% bound falls below zero from Nov 2023. This shows a weakness of classic additive structures on series in levels, compared with log-SARIMA. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hw_lb <- checkresiduals(hw_add) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ljung-Box test data: Residuals from Holt-Winters' additive method Q* = 107.62, df = 24, p-value = 1.464e-12 Model df: 0. Total lags used: 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual diagnostics, additive Holt-Winters](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-hw-resid-1.png){#fig-hw-resid width=768} ::: ::: The Ljung-Box test gives p = 1.46e-12 (< 0.05): the residuals are not white noise, with large dependencies at the seasonal lags (12, 24, 36). Holt-Winters makes the seasonal component too rigid and does not remove the seasonal memory of the index; on in-sample residual diagnostics it is inferior to SARIMA. ## Seasonal naive benchmark ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} naive_model <- snaive(ip_train, h = h) autoplot(naive_model) + autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") + labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Seasonal naive forecast against the test data](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-snaive-1.png){#fig-snaive width=768} ::: ::: The seasonal naive forecast repeats the last observed seasonal cycle with a flat trend. It captures the monthly pattern but cannot adapt to changes in the trend, and its intervals are wide. It is the basic benchmark that more complex models must beat. ## Model comparison Each model was estimated on the training data only and forecasts the 106 months of the test period, which are compared with the actual values. ::: {#tbl-accuracy .cell tbl-cap='Forecast accuracy on the test set (Jul 2016 to Apr 2025)'} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_trim <- sarima_real$mean[1:h] ets_trim <- ets_forecast$mean[1:h] hw_trim <- hw_add$mean[1:h] naive_trim <- naive_model$mean[1:h] acc_table <- rbind( SARIMA = accuracy(sarima_trim, ip_test)[1, ], ETS = accuracy(ets_trim, ip_test)[1, ], HOLT_WINTERS = accuracy(hw_trim, ip_test)[1, ], SNAIVE = accuracy(naive_trim, ip_test)[1, ] ) round(acc_table, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ME RMSE MAE MPE MAPE ACF1 Theil's U SARIMA 0.1194 2.9260 1.7876 0.0258 1.8382 0.8183 1.3290 ETS 6.0648 6.9336 6.4773 5.9659 6.4523 0.8404 2.9332 HOLT_WINTERS 7.0010 8.2455 7.4029 6.9009 7.3754 0.8883 3.4925 SNAIVE 0.6704 3.1476 2.2613 0.5816 2.3026 0.7934 1.3995 ``` ::: ::: 1. SARIMA has the smallest errors: RMSE = 2.926 and MAPE = 1.84%. 2. ETS (MAPE = 6.45%) and Holt-Winters (MAPE = 7.38%) systematically underestimate the test data. 3. SARIMA also beats the seasonal naive benchmark (MAPE = 2.3%). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} to_test_ts <- function(x) ts(x[1:h], start = start(ip_test), frequency = 12) autoplot(ip_ts, series = "Actual") + autolayer(to_test_ts(sarima_real$mean), series = "SARIMA", linewidth = 1) + autolayer(to_test_ts(ets_forecast$mean), series = "ETS", linewidth = 1) + autolayer(to_test_ts(hw_add$mean), series = "Holt-Winters", linewidth = 1) + autolayer(to_test_ts(naive_model$mean), series = "Seasonal naive", linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Forecasts over the test period](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-comparison-1.png){#fig-comparison width=768} ::: ::: The chart is consistent with the accuracy table. SARIMA follows the level and the fluctuations of the actual series closely, around 100 index points. ETS and Holt-Winters drift downwards and underestimate the series, which explains their large errors. The seasonal naive forecast does reasonably well thanks to its flat trend but does not adapt to the dynamics of the series. This comparison rests on a **single forecast origin** (June 2016): each error is a forecast from 1 to 106 months ahead, and the result depends heavily on where the trend of each model happened to point in mid-2016. The errors are also strongly autocorrelated (first-order autocorrelation of 0.82 for SARIMA), so a Diebold-Mariano test that treats them as independent one-step errors would overstate the significance of the differences. A rolling-origin evaluation gives a more reliable comparison. ## Rolling-origin evaluation Here the models are re-estimated every month of the test period on all data available up to that month (an expanding window) and forecast the next 1 to 12 months, as an analyst updating the forecast every month would do. Each model keeps the specification selected on the training data; only its parameters are re-estimated. SARIMA forecasts are medians, as above. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} max_h <- 12 sarima_order <- arimaorder(sarima_final) # Forecast functions with the specifications chosen on the training data ets_spec <- ets_auto$components # error, trend, season, damped forecast_functions <- list( SARIMA = function(x, h) { forecast(Arima(x, order = sarima_order[c("p", "d", "q")], seasonal = sarima_order[c("P", "D", "Q")], lambda = 0), h = h) }, ETS = function(x, h) { forecast(ets(x, model = paste0(ets_spec[1], ets_spec[2], ets_spec[3]), damped = as.logical(ets_spec[4])), h = h) }, `Holt-Winters` = function(x, h) hw(x, seasonal = "additive", h = h), `Seasonal naive` = function(x, h) snaive(x, h = h) ) # Row t, column k = error of the k-step forecast made with data up to month t. # The first origin is the end of the training sample (June 2016). cv_errors <- lapply(forecast_functions, function(f) { tsCV(ip_ts, f, h = max_h, initial = n_train - 1) }) # Actual value and target date of each k-step forecast, aligned with cv_errors n_obs <- length(ip_ts) target_value <- function(k) c(as.numeric(ip_ts)[-(1:k)], rep(NA, k)) target_time <- function(k) c(as.numeric(time(ip_ts))[-(1:k)], rep(NA, k)) cv_accuracy <- function(k, exclude_covid = FALSE) { keep <- !is.na(target_value(k)) if (exclude_covid) { keep <- keep & !(target_time(k) >= 2020 + 2 / 12 & target_time(k) < 2021.5) } t(sapply(cv_errors, function(E) { e <- E[, k] ok <- keep & !is.na(e) c(Forecasts = sum(ok), RMSE = sqrt(mean(e[ok]^2)), MAE = mean(abs(e[ok])), `MAPE (%)` = 100 * mean(abs(e[ok] / target_value(k)[ok]))) })) } cv_1 <- cv_accuracy(1) cv_12 <- cv_accuracy(12) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-cv-accuracy .cell tbl-cap='Rolling-origin accuracy, 1 and 12 months ahead'} ```{.r .cell-code} cv_table <- rbind( data.frame(Horizon = "1 month", Model = rownames(cv_1), round(cv_1, 3), check.names = FALSE), data.frame(Horizon = "12 months", Model = rownames(cv_12), round(cv_12, 3), check.names = FALSE) ) rownames(cv_table) <- NULL cv_table ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Horizon |Model | Forecasts| RMSE| MAE| MAPE (%)| |:---------|:--------------|---------:|-----:|-----:|--------:| |1 month |SARIMA | 106| 2.068| 1.115| 1.161| |1 month |ETS | 106| 1.964| 1.054| 1.094| |1 month |Holt-Winters | 106| 1.997| 1.086| 1.126| |1 month |Seasonal naive | 106| 4.105| 2.557| 2.630| |12 months |SARIMA | 95| 6.408| 3.479| 3.566| |12 months |ETS | 95| 6.501| 3.294| 3.375| |12 months |Holt-Winters | 95| 7.206| 3.709| 3.789| |12 months |Seasonal naive | 95| 4.309| 2.708| 2.789|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cv_rmse <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cv_errors), function(m) { data.frame( Model = m, Horizon = 1:max_h, RMSE = sapply(1:max_h, function(k) { e <- cv_errors[[m]][, k] sqrt(mean(e[!is.na(e) & !is.na(target_value(k))]^2)) }) ) })) ggplot(cv_rmse, aes(Horizon, RMSE, colour = Model)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:max_h) + labs(x = "Months ahead", y = "RMSE (index points)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Rolling-origin RMSE by forecast horizon](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-cv-rmse-1.png){#fig-cv-rmse width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rmse_of <- function(m) cv_rmse$RMSE[cv_rmse$Model == m] sarima_last_better <- max(which(rmse_of("SARIMA") < rmse_of("Seasonal naive"))) ets_last_better <- max(which(rmse_of("ETS") < rmse_of("Seasonal naive"))) ``` ::: The errors of the statistical models grow quickly with the horizon, while the seasonal naive error stays almost flat. SARIMA has a lower RMSE than the seasonal naive forecast up to 3 months ahead and ETS up to 4 months ahead; beyond that, repeating last year's values is more accurate on this sample. The 2020 pandemic produces a few very large errors that dominate the RMSE. As a robustness check, the table below excludes forecasts whose target month falls between March 2020 and June 2021: ::: {#tbl-cv-no-covid .cell tbl-cap='Rolling-origin accuracy excluding targets from March 2020 to June 2021'} ```{.r .cell-code} cv_1_nc <- cv_accuracy(1, exclude_covid = TRUE) cv_12_nc <- cv_accuracy(12, exclude_covid = TRUE) cv_table_nc <- rbind( data.frame(Horizon = "1 month", Model = rownames(cv_1_nc), round(cv_1_nc, 3), check.names = FALSE), data.frame(Horizon = "12 months", Model = rownames(cv_12_nc), round(cv_12_nc, 3), check.names = FALSE) ) rownames(cv_table_nc) <- NULL cv_table_nc ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

::: ::: ### Diebold-Mariano tests The Diebold-Mariano test compares the squared errors of SARIMA with those of each other model on the same forecast origins. The null hypothesis is equal accuracy; a negative statistic means SARIMA has smaller errors. For 12-month forecasts, consecutive errors overlap, and `h = 12` makes the test account for the resulting autocorrelation. ::: {#tbl-dm .cell tbl-cap='Diebold-Mariano tests on rolling-origin errors (SARIMA vs each model)'} ```{.r .cell-code} dm_rows <- list() for (k in c(1, max_h)) { for (m in setdiff(names(cv_errors), "SARIMA")) { a <- cv_errors$SARIMA[, k] b <- cv_errors[[m]][, k] ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b) test <- dm.test(a[ok], b[ok], alternative = "two.sided", h = k, power = 2) dm_rows[[length(dm_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame( Horizon = paste(k, if (k == 1) "month" else "months"), Comparison = paste("SARIMA vs", m), `DM statistic` = round(unname(test$statistic), 3), `p-value` = signif(test$p.value, 3), check.names = FALSE ) } } dm_table <- do.call(rbind, dm_rows) rownames(dm_table) <- NULL # Display copy with readable p-values dm_display <- dm_table dm_display[["p-value"]] <- ifelse( dm_table[["p-value"]] < 0.001, format(dm_table[["p-value"]], digits = 3, scientific = TRUE), sprintf("%.3f", dm_table[["p-value"]]) ) dm_display ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Horizon |Comparison | DM statistic|p-value | |:---------|:------------------------|------------:|:--------| |1 month |SARIMA vs ETS | 1.029|0.306 | |1 month |SARIMA vs Holt-Winters | 0.743|0.459 | |1 month |SARIMA vs Seasonal naive | -3.443|8.27e-04 | |12 months |SARIMA vs ETS | -0.549|0.584 | |12 months |SARIMA vs Holt-Winters | -1.110|0.270 | |12 months |SARIMA vs Seasonal naive | 1.041|0.300 |
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dm_p <- function(horizon, model) { dm_table[["p-value"]][dm_table$Horizon == horizon & dm_table$Comparison == paste("SARIMA vs", model)] } ``` ::: 1. **One month ahead**, SARIMA, ETS and Holt-Winters are very close (RMSE of 2.07 for SARIMA, 1.96 for ETS and 2.00 for Holt-Winters), and the Diebold-Mariano test does not distinguish SARIMA from ETS (p = 0.3060) or Holt-Winters (p = 0.4590). All three clearly beat the seasonal naive benchmark (RMSE 4.11; SARIMA vs seasonal naive p = 8.27e-04). 2. **Twelve months ahead**, the seasonal naive forecast has the lowest errors (RMSE 4.31 against 6.41 for SARIMA), but none of the differences is statistically significant (all p-values above 0.27). 3. Excluding the pandemic months lowers all errors substantially. One month ahead the three statistical models remain almost tied, and twelve months ahead the seasonal naive forecast is still the most accurate. The rolling-origin evaluation does **not** confirm the large advantage of SARIMA seen with a single forecast origin. At short horizons (one to a few months) the three statistical models perform equally well and all beat the seasonal naive benchmark; at a one-year horizon no model beats simply repeating the last year's values. ## Forecast beyond the sample The test period is only used to evaluate the models. To forecast the future, the selected SARIMA specification is re-estimated on the full sample (January 1990 to April 2025), so the forecast uses all the available data, including the years after 2016. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_full <- Arima( ip_ts, order = sarima_order[c("p", "d", "q")], seasonal = sarima_order[c("P", "D", "Q")], lambda = 0 # log transformation, as for the training model ) sarima_full ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Series: ip_ts ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] Box Cox transformation: lambda= 0 Coefficients: ar1 ar2 ar3 sma1 0.1495 -0.1557 0.0184 -0.7980 s.e. 0.0495 0.0492 0.0495 0.0323 sigma^2 = 0.000149: log likelihood = 1224.29 AIC=-2438.59 AICc=-2438.44 BIC=-2418.49 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} h_future <- 36 future <- forecast(sarima_full, h = h_future) # median forecast in index points autoplot(future, include = 120) + labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![SARIMA forecast for May 2025 to April 2028, estimated on the full sample](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-future-forecast-1.png){#fig-future-forecast width=768} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-future-forecast .cell tbl-cap='SARIMA forecast at selected horizons (index points)'} ```{.r .cell-code} future_steps <- c(6, 12, 24, 36) data.frame( Month = format(zoo::as.yearmon(time(future$mean)[future_steps])), `Months ahead` = future_steps, Forecast = round(future$mean[future_steps], 1), `80% interval` = sprintf("%.1f – %.1f", future$lower[future_steps, "80%"], future$upper[future_steps, "80%"]), `95% interval` = sprintf("%.1f – %.1f", future$lower[future_steps, "95%"], future$upper[future_steps, "95%"]), check.names = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Month | Months ahead| Forecast|80% interval |95% interval | |:--------|------------:|--------:|:------------|:------------| |Oct 2025 | 6| 101.9|97.9 – 106.0 |95.9 – 108.2 | |Apr 2026 | 12| 99.9|94.5 – 105.6 |91.8 – 108.7 | |Apr 2027 | 24| 100.3|92.1 – 109.4 |87.9 – 114.5 | |Apr 2028 | 36| 100.8|89.8 – 113.2 |84.5 – 120.3 |

The point forecast stays close to the recent level of the index, around 102 index points over the next 12 months, while the 95% interval widens from ±2.4 points one month ahead to about ±18 points after three years.
